blocks.text:
Design a parking lot system for a multi floor facility. Vehicles of different sizes arrive at entry gates, receive a ticket, park in a suitable spot, and pay based on the time parked when they leave through an exit gate.

The system must allocate the right spot for each vehicle type, track occupancy in real time, price each stay, and process payments, all while several gates operate concurrently. The design centres on clean entity modelling and swappable policies: how a spot is chosen and how a stay is priced are both strategies that change without touching the core.

  • Actors: drivers, entry and exit gates, and lot administrators
  • Scope: one physical lot with multiple floors and spot types, in memory, with a payment abstraction
  • Goal: an interview ready object oriented design that scales in floors, spots, and gates

Parking lot is the hello world of LLD: everyone knows the domain, so all the marks are for the design.

metadata.alt: Functional requirements at a glance: entry, exit, and the full case

items: Support multiple floors, each with spots of multiple types: bike, compact, large
Support vehicle types bike, car, and truck, each parkable only in compatible spots
Issue a ticket at entry recording vehicle, spot, and entry time
Find and allocate a free compatible spot automatically at entry
Reject entry with a clear FULL response when no compatible spot exists
Compute the fee at exit from the parked duration and vehicle type
Accept payment by cash or card, and open the exit gate only after successful payment
Free the spot on exit so it becomes available immediately
Show live availability counts per floor and per spot type

blocks.text: The lot may have thousands of spots and many simultaneous gates. Spot allocation must not scan the whole lot per arrival, and availability counters must be cheap to read.
New vehicle types, new spot types, new pricing rules, and new payment methods must be added as new classes or enum constants, not edits to tested code. Pricing especially changes often in real lots.
Each concept lives in its own small class. Policies, allocation and pricing, are isolated behind interfaces so business changes touch one file.
Entry and exit are user facing and must complete in constant or near constant time: allocation via per type free lists, ticket lookup via a hash map.
Multiple entry gates race for the same spots. The check and occupy step on a spot must be atomic so two vehicles never receive the same spot, and counters must stay consistent.

items: Vehicle mix: which vehicle types, and can a small vehicle take a larger spot when its own type is full?
Pricing: flat hourly, per vehicle type rates, day caps, or lost ticket fees?
Payment: pay at exit gate, or pay stations before returning to the car?
Gates: how many simultaneous entry and exit gates must the design serve?
Reservations and subscriptions: in scope or future work?
Electric vehicles: are charging spots a requirement now?
Persistence: in memory acceptable, or must tickets survive a restart?

blocks.text: Assumed answers for this design: bikes, cars, and trucks; a vehicle may upgrade to a bigger spot when its own type is exhausted; hourly pricing per vehicle type; pay at exit; several concurrent gates; reservations, EV charging, and persistence discussed as extensions.

items: Money is integer cents; time uses monotonic timestamps from a single clock source
Every parked vehicle holds exactly one ticket; the ticket id is the key for exit
A spot holds exactly one vehicle; trucks need large spots, cars fit compact or large, bikes fit anywhere
Fees start at entry time and are rounded up to the next hour
Payment must succeed before the spot is released and the gate opens
Lost tickets incur a fixed penalty fee, handled as a pricing special case
State is in memory; the database section shows the persistent schema

metadata.alt: The core entities and how they connect

items: ParkingLot: the facade and coordinator; owns floors and the policy strategies
ParkingFloor: a floor holding spots grouped by type for fast allocation
ParkingSpot: one space with a type and an occupied flag; the unit of contention
Vehicle hierarchy: abstract Vehicle with Bike, Car, and Truck subclasses
Ticket: immutable record of plate, spot, and entry time, issued at entry
Receipt: the exit record with the amount paid
SpotAllocationStrategy: policy for choosing which free spot to assign
PricingStrategy: policy for turning a ticket and exit time into a fee
PaymentStrategy: how the fee is collected, cash or card
EntryGate and ExitGate: thin controllers that drive the lot API

blocks.text: The two policy interfaces, allocation and pricing, are the levers of this design: they are where real lots differ, so they are exactly what we abstract.

8.1 What to say while drawing this
blocks.content: 8.1 What to say while drawing this

blocks.text: Start at ParkingLot and stress that it is a coordinator, not a god class: allocation and pricing decisions are delegated to strategies, and the mutable state lives in the spots.
The parts below take this one piece at a time, beginning with Strategy Pattern (allocation and pricing).

Why needed: which free spot to pick and how to price a stay are business policies that vary per lot and change over time: nearest first today, distribute by floor load tomorrow; hourly today, day caps and weekend rates tomorrow.
Why it is the best choice: a policy is a swappable algorithm behind a stable interface, which is precisely Strategy. Hard coding either policy would force edits to the lot for every business change.
What it solves: the lot calls findSpot and calculate without knowing the rules, so policy changes are new classes with zero risk to the core.
Why needed: the physical facility is one shared resource that all gates must see consistently; two lot instances would double allocate spots.
Why acceptable: a thread safe singleton, or one instance managed by dependency injection, guarantees a single source of truth. Prefer injection in production for testability, and say so.
Why needed: gates receive a plate and a type string from hardware and must construct the right Vehicle subclass.
What it solves: centralises construction so adding an ElectricCar touches the factory and nothing else.
Why needed: gates should call one simple interface, parkVehicle and unparkVehicle, rather than orchestrating floors, spots, strategies, and payments themselves. ParkingLot is that facade.
Strategy for the policies, Singleton for the shared facility, Factory for construction, Facade for a clean front door.

blocks.text: Why these abstractions exist: each captures a decision that varies independently of the core flow. The lot depends on the three interfaces and never on a concrete policy, so the dependency arrows point at abstractions and the core is closed against policy churn.

Why findAndClaim rather than find then claim: combining the search and the atomic claim in one interface method prevents the time gap where two gates find the same spot before either claims it. The interface itself encodes the concurrency contract.
Design the interface around the invariant: allocation must return a spot that is already yours.

A full lot must fail fast and change nothing. Allocation returns null, the gate shows FULL, and no ticket or spot state is touched.

metadata.alt: The failure categories and their exceptions

items: Unknown ticket id at exit: InvalidTicketException with the offending id
Duplicate plate trying to enter while already parked: DuplicateEntryException
No compatible spot free: LotFullException carrying the vehicle type, gate shows FULL

items: Two entry gates racing for the last free spot of a type
An exit freeing a spot while an entry is allocating, which must simply interleave safely

blocks.text: The invariant is that a spot flips from free to occupied exactly once per stay. Everything else, counters and free lists, follows from making that flip atomic and adjusting shared structures inside the same critical section or with atomic operations.

codes.python:
import threading


class SpotType:
    SMALL, COMPACT, LARGE = "small", "compact", "large"


class Vehicle:
    pass                                    # full hierarchy shown in a later block


class ParkingSpot:
    def __init__(self, spot_id: str, spot_type: str):
        self._spot_id = spot_id
        self._type = spot_type
        self._occupied = False
        self._vehicle = None
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def try_occupy(self, vehicle: Vehicle) -> bool:
        # the single atomic point of contention: check-and-set under one lock
        with self._lock:
            if self._occupied:
                return False        # another gate got here first
            self._occupied = True
            self._vehicle = vehicle
            return True              # this gate won the spot

    def vacate(self) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._vehicle = None
            self._occupied = False


if __name__ == "__main__":
    spot = ParkingSpot("F1-C1", SpotType.COMPACT)
    print(spot.try_occupy(Vehicle()))  # True
    print(spot.try_occupy(Vehicle()))  # False

items: Compare and set on the spot occupied flag: lock free and contention friendly
Concurrent free lists per spot type, so allocation pops a candidate and confirms with tryOccupy
LongAdder or atomic counters per type for availability, updated beside the spot operations
The active tickets map is a ConcurrentHashMap keyed by ticket id

metadata.alt: Extensions plug into existing abstractions without edits

items: New vehicle or spot type: a new enum constant and its compatibility row; allocation adapts automatically
New pricing rules: a new PricingStrategy, day caps, weekend rates, or per floor premiums, swapped in without touching the lot
New allocation policy: a new SpotAllocationStrategy, for example spread load across floors or fill top floors first
Reservations: a ReservationService that pre claims spots through the same tryOccupy contract
EV charging: a CHARGING spot type plus a pricing decorator that adds energy cost
Subscriptions and passes: a pricing strategy that returns zero for valid passes
License plate recognition replacing paper tickets, keyed by plate instead of ticket id
A mobile app showing live availability from the same counters
Dynamic pricing by occupancy, just another PricingStrategy reading the counters

metadata.alt: How the design maps to SOLID

items: Single Responsibility: spots guard occupancy, floors organise spots, tickets record facts, strategies decide policy, and the lot only coordinates
Open Closed: pricing, allocation, payments, and vehicle types all extend by adding classes or constants; the entry and exit flows never change
Liskov Substitution: any Vehicle subclass parks through the same flow; any strategy implementation drops in without the lot noticing
Interface Segregation: three small policy interfaces with one or two methods each; gates see only the lot facade
Dependency Inversion: the lot depends on SpotAllocationStrategy, PricingStrategy, and PaymentStrategy abstractions, with concretes injected at construction

metadata.alt: The edge cases the design must survive

items: Lot completely full: entry rejected before any state changes; FULL display driven by counters
The last spot claimed simultaneously from two gates: compare and set lets exactly one win; the loser re-runs allocation
Exit within the first minutes: pricing rounds up to one hour, or applies a grace period if the policy says so
Clock skew between entry and exit: one clock source and monotonic timestamps prevent negative durations
Vehicle stays for days: duration based pricing with a day cap policy handles long stays
A car takes a large spot when compact is full, then a truck arrives: acceptable under the upgrade policy; a stricter reserve policy is a strategy swap
Duplicate exit scans: the ticket closes on the first settle and the second scan is rejected
Spot marked out of service: removed from the free list, invisible to allocation, restored by admin

unparkVehicle: O(1), a hash lookup of the ticket, constant time pricing, and a spot flag flip

addFloor: O(S) to index the new floor spots into the free lists, done once
O(S) for S spots across all floors, each a small object
O(A) for A active tickets, bounded by S
O(1) additional per operation; nothing grows with historical traffic in memory

items: Keep per floor free lists sorted by distance from the gate to genuinely give the nearest spot
Batch counter reads for display boards to avoid hot atomic reads on large fleets
Shard free lists per gate to reduce contention at rush hour, rebalancing occasionally
How would you add reservations? Pre claim via the same atomic tryOccupy under a hold with expiry
How would valet or multi lot support change the model? A LotManager above multiple ParkingLot facades

Many lots report to a central service for citywide availability; each lot remains autonomous on its gates
Ticket ids become globally unique with a lot prefix; payments reconcile centrally and idempotently
The on premise design keeps working offline and syncs when the link returns

blocks.text: The full Java implementation in dependency order: enums, vehicles, spots and floors, strategies, tickets, and the lot facade with a runnable demo.

codes.python:
import threading
from collections import deque
from enum import Enum
from typing import Dict, List, Optional


class VehicleType(Enum):
    BIKE = "bike"
    CAR = "car"
    TRUCK = "truck"


class SpotType(Enum):
    SMALL = "small"
    COMPACT = "compact"
    LARGE = "large"

    @staticmethod
    def compatible(v: VehicleType) -> List["SpotType"]:
        # which spot types can host a vehicle type, in preferred order (shown in an earlier block)
        if v == VehicleType.BIKE:
            return [SpotType.SMALL, SpotType.COMPACT, SpotType.LARGE]
        if v == VehicleType.CAR:
            return [SpotType.COMPACT, SpotType.LARGE]
        if v == VehicleType.TRUCK:
            return [SpotType.LARGE]
        raise ValueError(f"unknown type {v}")


class Vehicle:                              # full hierarchy shown in an earlier block
    def __init__(self, vehicle_type: VehicleType):
        self._type = vehicle_type

    def get_type(self) -> VehicleType: return self._type


class ParkingSpot:
    def __init__(self, spot_id: str, spot_type: SpotType):
        self._spot_id = spot_id
        self._type = spot_type
        self._occupied = False
        self._vehicle: Optional[Vehicle] = None
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def get_id(self) -> str: return self._spot_id
    def get_type(self) -> SpotType: return self._type

    def try_occupy(self, vehicle: Vehicle) -> bool:     # atomic claim
        with self._lock:
            if self._occupied:
                return False
            self._occupied = True
            self._vehicle = vehicle
            return True

    def vacate(self) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._vehicle = None
            self._occupied = False


class ParkingFloor:
    def __init__(self, floor_number: int):
        self._floor_number = floor_number
        self._free_spots: Dict[SpotType, deque] = {t: deque() for t in SpotType}

    def add_spot(self, spot: ParkingSpot) -> None:
        self._free_spots[spot.get_type()].append(spot)

    def find_and_claim(self, vehicle_type: VehicleType, vehicle: Vehicle) -> Optional[ParkingSpot]:
        # pop candidates until one is atomically claimed
        for spot_type in SpotType.compatible(vehicle_type):
            queue = self._free_spots[spot_type]
            while queue:
                spot = queue.popleft()
                if spot.try_occupy(vehicle):
                    return spot      # claimed, done
                # lost the race for this spot; keep trying others
        return None                  # floor full for this type

    def release(self, spot: ParkingSpot) -> None:
        spot.vacate()
        self._free_spots[spot.get_type()].append(spot)  # back on the free list

    def get_floor_number(self) -> int: return self._floor_number


if __name__ == "__main__":
    floor = ParkingFloor(1)
    floor.add_spot(ParkingSpot("F1-C1", SpotType.COMPACT))
    floor.add_spot(ParkingSpot("F1-L1", SpotType.LARGE))

    car = Vehicle(VehicleType.CAR)
    claimed = floor.find_and_claim(VehicleType.CAR, car)
    print(f"Claimed: {claimed.get_id()}")
    floor.release(claimed)
    print(f"Released back to floor {floor.get_floor_number()}")

26.1 Free lists versus scanning for allocation
blocks.content: 26.1 Free lists versus scanning for allocation

blocks.text: Scanning floors per arrival is simple but O(S) under load. Per type concurrent free lists give O(1) allocation at the cost of maintaining them on release. For thousands of spots the lists win decisively.
26.2 Compare and set spots versus floor level locks
blocks.content: 26.2 Compare and set spots versus floor level locks

blocks.text: A lock per floor is easier to reason about but serialises every arrival on that floor. CAS per spot allows gates to proceed in parallel and only contend on the exact same spot, which is rare.
26.3 Ticket ids versus plate keyed stays
blocks.content: 26.3 Ticket ids versus plate keyed stays

blocks.text: Paper tickets are the classic interview model and support anonymous parking. Plate recognition removes ticket loss entirely but adds camera infrastructure and a privacy discussion. The core flows are identical either way.
26.4 Upgrade policy versus strict spot matching
blocks.content: 26.4 Upgrade policy versus strict spot matching

blocks.text: Letting cars take large spots improves utilisation but can starve trucks at peak times. A reserved quota per type is a middle ground, and because allocation is a strategy, all three policies are drop in swaps.

A singleton guarantees one source of truth but hides dependencies and hurts tests. Constructing one instance and injecting it keeps the same guarantee with better testability; say this trade off out loud.

items: Persistence first: tickets and spot states in a database with transactional exit settlement, so restarts never lose stays
Idempotent payments: retries carry the ticket id as an idempotency key so a driver is never double charged
Gate hardware faults: if the barrier fails after payment, the receipt is proof; staff override uses the closed ticket record
Monitoring: occupancy per type, allocation failures, payment failure rates, and gate latencies on dashboards
Reconciliation: nightly job matches payments to closed tickets and flags mismatches
Capacity planning: counters feed a FULL sign well before literal exhaustion, keeping cars from queueing inside
Testing: a concurrency test that storms one remaining spot from many threads and asserts exactly one ticket is issued
Graceful degradation: if pricing config fails to load, fall back to a safe default rate and alert, never free parking by accident

blocks.text: Model the contention point, abstract the policies, and keep money and state changes in one transaction. That is the parking lot in one sentence.
